title: C# Login Project · Start from Scratch
intro: Catch up on the key A Level ideas. Complete four retrieval questions, work through the examples, then practise and explain your reasoning.

questions.prompt: Choose the model answer: A rising-edge-triggered D-type flip-flop has Q = 0 and D = 1. What happens to Q when the next rising edge occurs?
questions.answer: Q becomes 1 at the rising edge because the flip-flop samples D. It then holds that value until the next triggering edge.
options: D is at the top. From top to bottom the stack is D, B, A. C was removed by the pop.

questions.prompt: Choose the model answer: Using 8-bit two’s complement, write −13 and explain why simply putting 1 before the 7-bit magnitude is not correct.
questions.answer: 13 = 00001101₂. Invert to 11110010₂, then add 1: 11110011₂. Prefixing the magnitude gives sign-and-magnitude (10001101₂), not two’s complement.

blocks.title: What must a login program do?
blocks.text: Read two inputs, decide whether both match the demonstration account, and show a clear result. Design the sequence before typing code.

blocks.title: Why start with sequence?
blocks.text: Read username; read password; display what was entered only during debugging. In the final version never echo a password.

blocks.title: Introduce selection
blocks.text: Use AND (&&) to require BOTH username and password to match. One wrong value must mean access denied.

blocks.title: Make a second attempt possible
blocks.text: A loop can repeat after invalid credentials. Add a maximum number of attempts to avoid an endless loop.

blocks.title: Worked example · Model the first three lines — not the finished program
blocks.text: Start in a blank .NET Fiddle console project. Predict what each statement does.

blocks.title: Worked example · Create a console program
blocks.text: using System; Console.Write("Username: "); string username = Console.ReadLine() ?? "";
